title: PID Feedback Loop Tuner
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Robotics and Computational Thinking
description: A 10-second strip chart shows a simulated robot turning from 0 to 90 degrees under PID control. Students adjust Kp, Ki, and Kd independently, compare each new curve with the previous one, and read live overshoot, settling time, final error, and P, I, and D term values.
source: Extends the proportional step-response idea of https://github.com/dmccreary/control-systems/tree/main/docs/sims/feedback-loop-simulator

educational.topic: PID control of a robot's heading
learningObjectives: Apply the PID formula by adjusting Kp, Ki, and Kd independently.
Describe how raising Kp speeds up the approach but increases overshoot and oscillation.
Describe how Kd damps overshoot and how Ki removes a steady-state error.
Measure overshoot, settling time, and final error from a step-response curve.
prerequisites: Reading line graphs of a value over time
standards: NGSS HS-ETS1-4: Use a computer simulation to model the impact of proposed solutions to a complex real-world problem.

controls.label: Step Target
controls.purpose: Replay the 0 to 90 degree target jump in real time with the current gains.

controls.label: Reset
controls.purpose: Restore Kp = 0.2, Ki = 0, Kd = 0 and clear the comparison curve.

simulationModel.modelType: Discrete-time PID control of a second-order heading model
equations: output = Kp*e + Ki*(sum of e*dt) - Kd*(d heading/dt), limited to +/-30
turn rate approaches 6*(output + drag) with a 0.4 s time constant
heading reading is delayed by 0.1 s; control loop runs at 50 Hz
assumptions: One wheel drags while driving, adding a constant -1.5 to the controller output.
The integral stops growing while the output is at its limit (anti-windup).
The derivative is taken from the heading, so the target jump does not cause a spike.
limitations: Heading wrap-around is not needed because the target only moves from 0 to 90 degrees.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Parameter exploration with immediate, quantified feedback and before/after comparison
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Three gain sliders, a comparison ghost curve, and live metric and term readouts
keyQuestions: Why does P-only control stop short of the target?
Which gain removes overshoot, and what happens if it is too large?
Why does a large Ki cause a big overshoot?
commonMisconceptions: A larger Kp always gives a better result.
The I term makes the robot faster (it removes leftover error, and too much adds overshoot).
Overshoot means the code has a bug (it is a normal consequence of gain and delay).
assessmentOpportunities: Record overshoot, settling time, and final error for several Kp values.
Find the smallest Kd that removes overshoot at Kp = 1.0.
Tuning challenge: under 10% overshoot, under 2 s settling, under 1 degree final error.
